description_full: Mueller Water Products, Inc. manufactures and markets products and services for the transmission, distribution, and measurement of water in the United States, Canada, and internationally. The company offers specialty valves and service brass products; and valves for water systems, including iron gate, butterfly, tapping, check, knife, plug, and ball valves used to control distribution and transmission of potable water and non-potable water, as well as water treatment facilities or industrial applications. It is also involved in the sale of pipe repair products, such as couplings, grips, and clamps used to repair leaks; produces machines and tools for tapping, drilling, extracting, installing and line stopping, as well as gas valve products use in gas distribution systems; and develops technologies and offers products and services that can non-invasively detect underground leaks and assess the condition of water mains comprised of a variety of materials. In addition, the company provides dry-barrel and wet-barrel fire hydrants; fixed leak detection systems that allow customers to continuously monitor and detect leaks on water distribution and transmission mains; intelligent water solutions comprising pressure control valves, advanced pressure management, network analytics, event management, and data logging; and residential, fire protection, and commercial metering solution comprising automatic meter reading and advanced metering infrastructure systems. It sells its products under the Canada Valve, Centurion, Echologics, Echoshore, ePulse, Ez-Max, Hersey, Hydro Gate, Hydro-Guard, HYMAX, HYMAX VERSA, Jones, Krausz, LeakFinderRT, Milliken, Mueller, Mueller Systems, Pratt, Pratt Industrial, Repaflex, Repamax, Sentryx, Singer, and U.S. Pipe Valve and Hydrant brands. Its products are used by municipalities, and residential and non-residential construction industries. Mueller Water Products, Inc. was founded in 1857 and is headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.

financial_summary: MUELLER WATER PRODUCTS is a mid-cap industrials business with a $3.7B market cap on $1.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 32%.

The business throws off $207M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.18× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 77× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 2.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 11pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.77x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+8.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 24% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 0.96, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.18 vs 5y 0.95), so read it loosely.
About $29.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 44% in the 2020 crash, 29% in the 2022 bear market and 87% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $23.51 (margin of safety -0%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 35%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $17.81 to $31.71 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 16.8 vs 22.1 and EV/EBITDA 9.8 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 11% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $27.83 on average, 18% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 9.3%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.40).
It runs a 32% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.18x.
ROE of 19% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 6pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 1.3% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $112.2M (3% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.3, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 141 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.0% over 3 years, 5.8% over 5 years and 2.6% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 85% of profits supports about 9.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 17.1% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 3.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 4 purchases and 7 sales over the past year, net $2.5M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 2.0% (0.8% in buybacks and 1.4% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 19 consecutive years, raising it 5.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 3,300 employees, each generates about $447K of revenue, 1.2x the Industrials median.
That works out to $63K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.9M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
